newsitem.title: CANADA: GM Canada striking workers dig in, city braces.
newsitem.headline: GM Canada striking workers dig in, city braces.

text.p: Striking workers huddled around wood fires burning in trash cans outside the sprawling General Motors Corp. complex that sat idled after the walkout began late on Wednesday night.

While striking members of the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union complained about the world's biggest automaker, shopowners and citizens of Canada's "Motor City" braced for a long and potentially devasting strike that could devastate the economy in this small city on Lake Ontario in southeastern Ontario.

Friends and GM pensioners drove by honking their horns in support of the strike, which began Wednesday night. About one out of six jobs in the nation's richest and most populous province is tied to the auto industry.

Flanked by security cameras at the gates and television crews on the streets, many complained they were caught between a public perception of "lazy" auto workers and long hours that have hurt their bodies, spirits and family lives while GM Canada earned nearly $1.4 billion in profits last year.

"It's the management's attitude that has put us out here," said 33-year old David Neely, who said he normally starts work at 7:30 p.m. and ends around 3:30 a.m., making it difficult to find time to spend with his 4-year-old son.
"When my son comes by (the plant) he says, 'my daddy works in prison," pointing to the barbed wire fences.
About 14,000 workers struck GM Canada in Oshawa and another 1,500 at Ste-Therese in Quebec. No progress was reported in talks Thursday and the strike looked set to last at least another day.
Gayle Evans said unusual shifts and mandatory overtime make it hard for plant workers to have normal lives or relationships.
"We have a very high divorce rate here," she said. "Many of the people here, including me, have a hard time because they are always here."
Bar owners said it was a bitter way to see an increase in their businesses and school principals mused about the impact on the children.

"They have really been pushed to the wall in last year," said Jim Peios, owner of Gorky's Bar and Restaurant, which was full on Wednesday night after workers walked out two hours ahead of the midnight strike deadline.
"It was party time last night," he said.

But a five-minute drive from Gorky's, school principal Paddy Cauley worried about the toll a long-term strike could take on the children racing around him into Monsignor Philip Coffey elementary school.
"If this were to go on for any extended length of time we would start planning to see how we could help," Cauley said.
He said the kids would have trouble understanding tensions at home from the strike over like grocery bills or renting a movie.
"If it means cutting back on things like movies and possibly food, then that's going to have an impact," he said.
Striking union members will get C$125 ($92) a week from the union, a big cut for workers who are paid C$22 ($16) an hour, or C$880 ($640) for 40 hours of work.

The ripple effect on the outlying community is expected to be devastating for small businesses, auto parts suppliers and even hair salons, already feeling the pinch from provincial government cutbacks.
"I think it's going to put every business that's weak out of business," said Dave Kortekaas, manager of The Hairchamber as he stood in front of rows of empty chairs and sinks.
"We've had less (business) since welfare went down and now with GM we'll get even less," said Jackie Glenn, the only hair dresser on duty.

But Ken Tower, manager of the Save-A-Buck Discount store, said shoppers who would normally cruise into high-end stores to buy everyday items would be more likely to slip into his store. "I guess they'll have to watch their money," he said.

The strike began after GM Canada refused to accept limitations on outsourcing -- the use of outside, usually non-union workers -- which the CAW had agreed on with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit two weeks ago.
